title: XLOOKUP
description: Looks up a value in one range and returns the matching value from another range.

arguments.name: lookup_value
arguments.description: The value to search for.

arguments.name: lookup_array
arguments.description: The range or array to search in.

arguments.name: return_array
arguments.description: The range or array to return a value from.

arguments.name: if_not_found
arguments.description: Text to return when no match is found. If left out, #N/A is returned.
arguments.clause: If there is no match, it shows {if_not_found} instead of #N/A.

arguments.name: match_mode
arguments.description: How to match: 0 exact (default), -1 exact or next smaller, 1 exact or next larger, 2 wildcard match.
arguments.clause: A match_mode of {match_mode} sets how close a match must be (0 means exact).

arguments.name: search_mode
arguments.description: Search direction: 1 first to last (default), -1 last to first, 2 binary search on data sorted ascending, -2 binary search on data sorted descending.
arguments.clause: A search_mode of {search_mode} sets the direction (1 searches first to last, -1 last to first).

taskPhrases: find employee information using an id
find employee by id
retrieve matching data from another table
look up a value in a table
get value from another sheet
notes: Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024. Microsoft notes it is not available in Excel 2016 or 2019.
Unlike VLOOKUP, the return column can be on either side of the lookup column, and return_array can span several columns to return more than one field.
explanation: Looks for {lookup_value} in {lookup_array} and returns the value in the same position from {return_array}.

title: VLOOKUP
description: Looks up a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from a column to the right.

arguments.name: lookup_value
arguments.description: The value to find in the first column of the table.

arguments.name: table_array
arguments.description: The table to search. The lookup column must be its first column.

arguments.name: col_index_num
arguments.description: Which column of the table to return (1 = first column).

arguments.name: range_lookup
arguments.description: Use FALSE for an exact match. TRUE (default) assumes sorted data and finds an approximate match.
arguments.clause: A range_lookup of {range_lookup} sets the match type: FALSE needs an exact match, TRUE finds the closest value (the first column must be sorted).

taskPhrases: find employee information using an id
find employee by id
retrieve matching data from another table
look up a price from a product code
notes: Leaving out FALSE means an approximate match, which assumes the first column is sorted and can give wrong results. Add FALSE for an exact match.
It can only look to the right of the lookup column. Use XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH, to look left.
If col_index_num is larger than the number of columns in table_array, you get #REF!.
Numbers or dates stored as text, and stray spaces, can cause wrong results. TRIM can help with spaces.
explanation: Looks for {lookup_value} in the first column of {table_array} and returns the value from column {col_index_num} of that row.

title: INDEX
description: Returns the value at a given row and column position within a range. Often combined with MATCH for flexible lookups.

arguments.name: array
arguments.description: The range to return a value from.

arguments.name: row_num
arguments.description: The row to return a value from. Required unless column_num is given.

arguments.name: column_num
arguments.description: The column to return a value from.
arguments.clause: It reads column {column_num} of that row.

taskPhrases: find employee information using an id
look up a value to the left of the search column
return the value at a row and column position
notes: In the example, MATCH finds the position and INDEX returns the value at that position. The 0 in MATCH means an exact match. If you leave it out, MATCH assumes 1 (approximate, sorted data), which can give wrong results.
Setting row_num or column_num to 0 returns the whole column or row.
explanation: Returns the value from {array} at the position given by {row_num}.

title: IF
description: Returns one value if a condition is true and another value if it is false.

arguments.name: logical_test
arguments.description: A condition that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

arguments.name: value_if_true
arguments.description: Result when the condition is TRUE.

arguments.name: value_if_false
arguments.description: Result when the condition is FALSE.
arguments.clause: If it is not, it shows {value_if_false}.

taskPhrases: show a different result depending on a value
label cells based on a condition
if this then that
notes: Text results must be in double quotes (TRUE and FALSE do not need them).
If value_if_true or value_if_false is left empty, the cell can show 0.
Many nested IFs get hard to read. Consider IFS or a lookup table instead.
explanation: Checks whether {logical_test} is true. If it is, it shows {value_if_true}.

title: IFERROR
description: Returns a custom value when a formula results in an error, otherwise returns the formula's result.

arguments.name: value
arguments.description: The formula or value to check for an error.

arguments.name: value_if_error
arguments.description: What to return if the formula produces an error.

taskPhrases: hide error messages in cells
replace #n/a with blank
show a friendly message instead of an error
avoid divide by zero error
notes: It hides all seven error types: #N/A, #VALUE!, #REF!, #DIV/0!, #NUM!, #NAME? and #NULL!. That includes real mistakes in your formula.
To hide only #N/A, use IFNA. For lookups, XLOOKUP also has its own if_not_found argument.
explanation: Calculates {value}. If that gives an error, it shows {value_if_error} instead.

title: SUMIFS
description: Adds up values that meet one or more conditions.

arguments.name: sum_range
arguments.description: The cells to add up.

arguments.name: criteria_range1
arguments.description: The range to test against the first condition.

arguments.name: criteria1
arguments.description: The first condition, such as "North" or ">100".

arguments.name: criteria_range2
arguments.description: A second range to test, if you need another condition. You can keep adding range and condition pairs.
arguments.clause: It also requires {criteria_range2} to match {criteria2}.

arguments.name: criteria2
arguments.description: The second condition, matched against criteria_range2.

taskPhrases: add up values that match a condition
total sales for a region
sum numbers if another column equals something
sum with multiple criteria
notes: The argument order differs from SUMIF: sum_range is first in SUMIFS but third in SUMIF. This is a common source of errors.
Every criteria range must have the same number of rows and columns as sum_range.
You can use up to 127 range and criteria pairs.
explanation: Adds up the values in {sum_range} where {criteria_range1} matches {criteria1}.

title: COUNTIF
description: Counts the cells in a range that meet a single condition.

arguments.name: range
arguments.description: The cells to check.

arguments.name: criteria
arguments.description: The condition, such as "Done", ">10", or a cell reference.

taskPhrases: count how many cells match a condition
count completed tasks
find duplicates in a list
count how many times a value appears
notes: It takes only one condition. For more than one, use COUNTIFS.
It is not case-sensitive, so "done" and "DONE" match.
In criteria, ? matches one character, * matches any run of characters, and ~ before them matches the symbol itself.
Text criteria longer than 255 characters can give wrong results.
explanation: Counts the cells in {range} that match {criteria}.

title: TRIM
description: Removes extra spaces from text, leaving only single spaces between words.

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: The text or cell to clean.

taskPhrases: remove extra spaces from text
clean up messy data
lookup fails because of spaces
remove leading and trailing spaces
notes: TRIM removes the standard space (character 32). It does not remove the non-breaking space (character 160) that often comes from web pages. Replace it first: =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A2, CHAR(160), " ")).
explanation: Removes extra spaces from {text}, leaving single spaces between words.

title: TEXTJOIN
description: Combines text from multiple cells using a delimiter, optionally skipping empty cells.

arguments.name: delimiter
arguments.description: The separator between items: text in double quotes such as ", " or " ", or an empty string.

arguments.name: ignore_empty
arguments.description: TRUE skips empty cells. FALSE includes them, which can leave repeated separators.

arguments.name: text1
arguments.description: The first cell, range or text to join.

arguments.name: text2
arguments.description: More text or ranges to join. You can use up to 252 text items in total.
arguments.clause: It also joins {text2}.

taskPhrases: combine first and last name
join text from several cells
merge cells into one with commas
concatenate with a separator
notes: Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2019, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024, but not Excel 2016.
explanation: Joins {text1} into one cell, putting {delimiter} between items (ignore_empty is {ignore_empty}; TRUE skips empty cells).

title: UNIQUE
description: Returns the distinct values from a range, removing duplicates.

arguments.name: array
arguments.description: The range to extract unique values from.

arguments.name: by_col
arguments.description: TRUE compares columns and returns unique columns. The default, FALSE, compares rows.
arguments.clause: A by_col of {by_col} chooses what to compare: FALSE compares rows, TRUE compares columns.

arguments.name: exactly_once
arguments.description: TRUE returns only values that appear exactly once. The default, FALSE, returns every distinct value.
arguments.clause: An exactly_once of {exactly_once} chooses what to keep: TRUE keeps only values that appear exactly once.

taskPhrases: remove duplicates from a list
get a list of distinct values
list each value only once
find unique entries
notes: The result spills into neighbouring cells. If those cells are not empty, Excel shows a #SPILL! error.
Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024.
explanation: Lists each different value in {array} once.

title: SUM
description: Adds up numbers, cells or ranges.
explanation: Adds up the numbers in {number1}.

arguments.name: number1
arguments.description: The first number, cell or range to add.

arguments.name: number2
arguments.description: More numbers, cells or ranges to add. You can use up to 255 arguments in total.
arguments.clause: It also adds {number2}.

taskPhrases: add up a column of numbers
total a list
sum a range
add numbers together
calculate a total
notes: SUM ignores text in the cells it adds, so text does not cause a #VALUE! error the way + can.
You can use up to 255 arguments.
To add only the cells that meet a condition, use SUMIFS.

title: AVERAGE
description: Returns the average (mean) of numbers, cells or ranges.
explanation: Finds the average of the numbers in {number1}.

arguments.name: number1
arguments.description: The first number, cell or range to average.

arguments.name: number2
arguments.description: More numbers, cells or ranges to include. You can use up to 255 arguments in total.
arguments.clause: It also includes {number2}.

taskPhrases: find the average of a column
calculate the mean
average score
average of numbers
notes: Text, true/false values and empty cells inside a range are ignored. Cells that contain zero are counted.
Values typed straight into the formula behave differently: number-like text is not counted, and text that cannot be read as a number causes an error.
To include true/false values and number-like text, use AVERAGEA.

title: MAX
description: Returns the largest number in a set of values.
explanation: Finds the largest number in {number1}.

arguments.name: number1
arguments.description: The first number, cell or range to check.

arguments.name: number2
arguments.description: More numbers, cells or ranges to check. You can use up to 255 arguments in total.
arguments.clause: It also checks {number2}.

taskPhrases: find the highest value
find the largest number
get the biggest number in a column
top sales figure
notes: Text, true/false values and empty cells inside a range are ignored.
If there are no numbers at all, MAX returns 0.
To include true/false values and number-like text, use MAXA.

title: COUNTIFS
description: Counts the rows that meet all of several conditions.
explanation: Counts the rows where {criteria_range1} matches {criteria1}.

arguments.name: criteria_range1
arguments.description: The first range to test.

arguments.name: criteria1
arguments.description: The condition for criteria_range1, such as "Done" or ">10".

arguments.name: criteria_range2
arguments.description: A second range to test. You can keep adding range and condition pairs.
arguments.clause: It only counts rows where {criteria_range2} also matches {criteria2}.

arguments.name: criteria2
arguments.description: The condition for criteria_range2.

taskPhrases: count rows that meet two conditions
count completed tasks for one person
count with multiple criteria
how many rows match several conditions
notes: You can use up to 127 range and condition pairs.
Every range must have the same number of rows and columns as the first one. They do not have to be next to each other.
In conditions, ? matches one character, * matches any run of characters, and ~ before them matches the symbol itself.

title: MATCH
description: Finds where a value sits in a list and returns its position.
explanation: Finds the position of {lookup_value} in {lookup_array}.

arguments.name: lookup_value
arguments.description: The value to find.

arguments.name: lookup_array
arguments.description: The range to search.

arguments.name: match_type
arguments.description: How to match. 0 finds the first exact match. 1 (the default) finds the largest value that is less than or equal, in a list sorted ascending. -1 finds the smallest value that is greater than or equal, in a list sorted descending.
arguments.clause: A match_type of {match_type} sets how it matches: 0 means an exact match, 1 the closest smaller value (sorted ascending), -1 the closest larger value (sorted descending).

taskPhrases: find the row number of a value
get the position of an item in a list
where is this value in the column
notes: MATCH returns the position in the list, not the value itself. If nothing matches it returns #N/A.
If you leave match_type out it defaults to 1, which needs a sorted list and can give wrong results. Use 0 for an exact match.
It is not case-sensitive.
Wildcards (? and *) work only with match_type 0 and text values.

title: AND
description: Returns TRUE only if every condition is true.
explanation: Checks whether {logical1} is true.

arguments.name: logical1
arguments.description: The first condition to test.

arguments.name: logical2
arguments.description: More conditions to test. You can use up to 255 conditions in total.
arguments.clause: It also checks {logical2}. The result is TRUE only when all of the conditions are true.

taskPhrases: check that two conditions are both true
test several conditions at once
pass only if every condition is met
notes: AND is often used inside IF to test more than one condition at once.
Text and empty cells inside a range are ignored. If a range has no true/false values at all, AND returns #VALUE!.
You can use up to 255 conditions.

title: OR
description: Returns TRUE if at least one condition is true.
explanation: Checks whether {logical1} is true.

arguments.name: logical1
arguments.description: The first condition to test.

arguments.name: logical2
arguments.description: More conditions to test. You can use up to 255 conditions in total.
arguments.clause: It also checks {logical2}. The result is TRUE if any one of the conditions is true.

taskPhrases: check whether either condition is true
test if any of several conditions is met
notes: OR is often used inside IF to react when any one of several conditions is met.
Text and empty cells inside a range are ignored. If a range has no true/false values at all, OR returns #VALUE!.
You can use up to 255 conditions.

title: LEFT
description: Returns the first characters of a piece of text.
explanation: Takes text from the start of {text}.

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: The text, or the cell that contains it.

arguments.name: num_chars
arguments.description: How many characters to take. If left out, it takes 1.
arguments.clause: It takes the first {num_chars} characters.

taskPhrases: get the first few characters of a cell
extract the first 3 letters
take the start of a code
notes: If num_chars is left out, LEFT returns just the first character.
num_chars must be zero or more. If it is longer than the text, LEFT returns all of the text.

title: FILTER
description: Returns only the rows or columns that meet a condition.
explanation: Returns the rows of {array} where {include} is true.

arguments.name: array
arguments.description: The range to filter.

arguments.name: include
arguments.description: A true/false test with the same number of rows (or columns) as array. The rows where it is true are kept.

arguments.name: if_empty
arguments.description: What to show if nothing matches.
arguments.clause: If nothing matches, it shows {if_empty} instead of an error.

examples.result: 2 rows: Ana Lim and Dev Patel

taskPhrases: show only the rows for one department
list every row that meets a condition
filter data with a formula
notes: The result spills into the cells below and to the right, so those cells need to be empty.
If nothing matches and you left out if_empty, Excel shows a #CALC! error. Add if_empty whenever the data might return no rows.
For two conditions that must both be true, multiply them: (B2:B5="Sales")*(C2:C5="North"). For either one, add them with +.
Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024.

title: SORT
description: Sorts the rows of a range in order.
explanation: Sorts the rows of {array} by its first column, smallest to largest.

arguments.name: array
arguments.description: The range to sort.

arguments.name: sort_index
arguments.description: The column (or row) number to sort by. If left out, it sorts by the first one.
arguments.clause: It sorts by column {sort_index} instead.

arguments.name: sort_order
arguments.description: 1 sorts ascending (the default). -1 sorts descending.
arguments.clause: A sort_order of {sort_order} sets the direction: 1 is smallest to largest, -1 is largest to smallest.

arguments.name: by_col
arguments.description: FALSE (the default) sorts rows. TRUE sorts columns.
arguments.clause: A by_col of {by_col} chooses what to sort: FALSE sorts rows, TRUE sorts columns.

examples.result: Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev (A to Z)

taskPhrases: sort a list alphabetically
order rows from highest to lowest
sort data with a formula
notes: The result spills into neighbouring cells, so those cells need to be empty.
The sorted result has the same shape as the original range.
Microsoft recommends SORTBY for sorting grids, because SORTBY keeps working when columns are added or removed.
Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024.

title: AutoSum
description: Add up a column or row of numbers with one shortcut.
steps: Click the empty cell directly below a column of numbers, or just to the right of a row of numbers.
Press the shortcut. Excel inserts a SUM formula and highlights the numbers it will add.
Press Enter to confirm and show the total.
taskPhrases: add up a column quickly
total a row of numbers
insert a sum formula with a shortcut
sum shortcut
notes: AutoSum is also a button on the Home tab, and under Formulas > AutoSum.
Check the highlighted range before you press Enter. If it is wrong, you can edit the formula.
If you copy an AutoSum formula to another cell, its references adjust to the new location.

title: Jump to the edge of your data
description: Hold Ctrl and press an arrow key to jump straight to the edge of the data.
steps: Click a cell inside your data.
Hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) and press an arrow key. The selection jumps to the edge of the current data region in that direction.
To select everything on the way instead of just jumping, add Shift: Ctrl + Shift + Arrow key on Windows, or Shift + Cmd + Arrow key on Mac.
taskPhrases: jump to the bottom of a column
go to the last row of data
move to the end of the data quickly
skip to the edge of the table
notes: Ctrl + Shift + Arrow key (Shift + Cmd + Arrow key on Mac) extends the selection to the last nonblank cell in that row or column.
Ctrl + Home jumps to the start of the worksheet, and Ctrl + End jumps to the last used cell.

title: Data entry form
description: Open a simple form to add, find, edit and delete rows without scrolling sideways.
unofficial: The Alt, D, O key sequence is not listed on Microsoft’s pages. It is an old menu shortcut that community sources report still works in Windows Excel, but it may differ by version or language. The documented way is to add the Form button to the Quick Access Toolbar, as in the steps below.
steps: Make sure each column has a header and there are no blank rows in your data.
Click a cell inside the range or table.
Press Alt, then D, then O, one key at a time, to try the shortcut. If it does nothing in your version, use the Form button as described next.
To add the Form button: click the arrow next to the Quick Access Toolbar, choose More Commands, set Choose commands from to All Commands, select Form, click Add, then OK.
Click Form on the toolbar. Use New to add a row, Find Next and Find Prev to move between rows, and Delete to remove one.
taskPhrases: open a data entry form in excel
add rows without typing in the grid
enter records using a form
hidden data entry form
notes: Some guides say to select the header row first. Microsoft only requires that the range has headers and that you click a cell inside it.
A form handles up to 32 columns. If you see "Too many fields in the data form", insert a blank column to split the range in two.
Press Enter after typing to save a new row (it is added at the bottom of the range or table) or to update an edited row.
Formulas show their results in the form but cannot be changed there.
Once you confirm a delete in the form, it cannot be undone. You also cannot print the form, and it must be closed before you use Print.

title: Create a table
description: Turn a range of data into an Excel table.
steps: Click any cell inside your data.
Press the shortcut to open the Create Table dialog box.
Check the range Excel suggests, then confirm.
taskPhrases: turn data into a table
make a table from a range
format data as a table
notes: On Windows, Ctrl + L does the same thing.
On Mac, Ctrl + T also works.

title: Insert today’s date
description: Enter the current date in a cell with one shortcut.
steps: Click the cell where you want the date.
Press the shortcut. Excel enters the current date.
taskPhrases: put todays date in a cell
insert the current date
enter the date quickly
notes: To enter the current time instead, press Ctrl + Shift + : on Windows, or Cmd + ; on Mac.

title: Fill down
description: Copy the cell above into the selected cells below.
steps: Select the cell you want to copy, plus the empty cells below it.
Press the shortcut. The top cell’s contents and format are copied down.
taskPhrases: copy a formula down a column
repeat the value above
fill cells with the cell above
notes: On Mac, Ctrl + D also works.

title: Repeat the last action
description: Repeat what you just did, such as a fill colour or inserting a row, on the next cell or row.
steps: Do the action once, for example fill a cell with colour or insert a row.
Click the next cell, or select the next row, where you want the same thing.
Press F4. Excel repeats the last action, so you do not need to click the button or right-click again.
taskPhrases: repeat the last thing i did
apply the same fill colour to other cells
insert rows in several places without right clicking
notes: Excel repeats the action only if it can. Some actions cannot be repeated.
Ctrl + Y does the same on Windows.
While you are editing a formula, F4 switches a cell reference between absolute and relative instead.
Microsoft lists no repeat shortcut for Mac. There, Cmd + Y is Redo.

title: Format Painter
description: Copy a cell’s formatting onto many other cells without picking the brush up each time.
steps: Select a cell that has the formatting you want to copy.
On the Home tab, in the Clipboard group, double-click Format Painter.
Click or drag across each cell or range you want to format. The brush stays on, so you can keep going.
When you are done, press Esc or click Format Painter again to turn it off.
taskPhrases: copy formatting to several cells
apply the same formatting to different places
keep the format painter on
notes: A single click on Format Painter applies the formatting once. Double-clicking keeps it on.

title: Flash Fill
description: Type the first result by hand and let Excel spot the pattern and fill in the rest of the column.
steps: Keep the data you are working from in one column, and leave the column next to it empty.
In the first cell of the empty column, type the result you want for the first row, for example a full name, and press Enter.
Press Ctrl + E, or choose Data, then Flash Fill. Excel spots the pattern and fills the cells below.
On Windows you can also start typing the second result. Excel shows a preview of the rest of the column, and pressing Enter accepts it.
taskPhrases: split first and last names into separate columns
combine first and last names
fill a column from a pattern
extract part of the text in a cell
notes: Flash Fill works by sensing a pattern in what you type, so your first example needs to show the pattern clearly.
If the preview does not appear, check that Automatically Flash Fill is ticked under Options, Advanced, Editing Options. You can always run it yourself with Ctrl + E.

title: Lock cell references
description: Switch a reference between relative and absolute so it stays put when you copy a formula.
steps: Press F2 on a cell (or click in the formula bar) and put the cursor on a reference such as A2.
Press the shortcut. The reference cycles through combinations such as $A$2, A$2 and $A2.
Keep pressing until you have the one you want, then press Enter.
taskPhrases: add dollar signs to a reference
stop a cell reference from changing when copied
lock a cell in a formula
notes: A $ in front of a column letter or row number stops that part from changing when you copy the formula.
On Mac, F4 also works.

title: Show all formulas
description: Switch the sheet between showing each formula’s result and showing the formulas themselves.
steps: Click the worksheet you want to look at.
Press Ctrl + ` (the grave accent key, usually the one above Tab, shared with ~). Every cell with a formula now shows the formula instead of its result.
Press the same keys again to switch back.
taskPhrases: see all the formulas on a sheet at once
show formulas instead of results
switch between formulas and values
notes: It switches the whole worksheet, not just the cells you have selected.

title: Select a row or column
description: Select a whole row or a whole column from the keyboard.
unofficial: Microsoft does not say what Shift + Space does inside an Excel table. Community guides report that it selects just the table row first and the whole worksheet row on a second press, but that can vary, so try it in your version.
steps: Click any cell in the row or column you want.
Press Shift + Space to select the whole row, or Ctrl + Space to select the whole column.
Inside an Excel table, press Ctrl + Space once to select only that table column’s data. Press it twice to select the whole table column, including its header.
To select the whole table instead, click inside it and press Ctrl + A. Press Ctrl + A twice to include the headers.
taskPhrases: select a whole row
select an entire column
highlight a whole column with the keyboard
select the whole table
notes: On Mac, Ctrl + Space conflicts with a default macOS shortcut. Microsoft says you may need to change or clear that macOS setting before Excel can use it.
Ctrl + Shift + Space selects the entire worksheet on Windows. If the sheet has data, the first press selects the current region, and pressing again widens the selection. On Mac, use Cmd + A.
Once a whole row or column is selected, you can insert, delete, hide or format it in one go.

title: Jump between a formula and its references
description: Select the cells a formula uses, then jump back to the formulas that use a cell.

keys.label: Select the cells a formula refers to
Select the formulas that refer to a cell

unofficial: Ctrl + [ and Ctrl + ] are not listed in Microsoft’s Windows shortcut list. They are long-standing Excel shortcuts that community guides report working in Windows Excel, but they may differ by version. The Mac keys are as Microsoft lists them, and they differ slightly from Windows. If a shortcut does nothing, use Go To Special as in the steps below.
steps: Click a cell that contains a formula.
Press Ctrl + [. Excel selects the cells that formula refers to. These are called its precedents.
To go back, select one of those referenced cells and press Ctrl + ]. Excel selects the formulas that refer to that cell. These are called its dependents.
If the shortcut does nothing in your version, press Ctrl + G, choose Special, then pick Precedents or Dependents. Choose Direct only for the first level, or All levels to follow the whole chain.
To see the links drawn as arrows instead, use Formulas > Trace Precedents or Trace Dependents.
taskPhrases: jump to the cell a formula refers to
find which cells a formula uses
see which formulas use this cell
go back to the formula from its source cell
trace where a formula gets its data
switch between a formula and its references
toggle between a formula and its source cells
move between a formula and the cells it uses
notes: Precedents are the cells a formula refers to. Dependents are the cells whose formulas refer to another cell. If D10 holds =B5, then B5 is a precedent of D10, and D10 is a dependent of B5.
On Mac, Microsoft also lists Ctrl + Shift + { and Ctrl + Shift + } to select every level of precedents and dependents.
Pressing F2 on a cell with a formula shows its precedents as colour-coded outlines.
Trace arrows are blue for cells without errors and red for cells that cause errors.

title: Show or hide gridlines
description: Turn the grid lines on a worksheet on or off from the keyboard.

keys.windows: Alt then W then V then G

unofficial: Alt, W, V, G is not listed in Microsoft’s shortcut list, which only gives Alt + W for opening the View tab. Long-standing Excel guides give W, V, G for View > Show > Gridlines, but check it in your version.
steps: Click the worksheet you want to change. Gridlines are set for each worksheet separately.
Press Alt and let go, then press W, then V, then G, one key at a time.
Run it again to bring the gridlines back.
If a letter does not match in your version, press Alt and follow the Key Tips (the small letters that appear on the ribbon) to the same command.
taskPhrases: remove the grid lines from a sheet
turn off gridlines
hide the gridlines in excel
show gridlines again
notes: It works as a switch: it hides the gridlines if they are showing and shows them if they are hidden.
It is the keyboard route to View > Show > Gridlines.
To change several sheets at once, select them first by holding Ctrl and clicking their tabs.

title: Add or remove borders
description: Put borders around every selected cell, or take them away, from the keyboard.

keys.label: Add borders to every cell
keys.windows: Alt then H then B then A

keys.label: Remove borders
keys.windows: Alt then H then B then N

keys.label: More borders (opens the Format Cells dialog)
keys.windows: Alt then H then B then M

unofficial: Microsoft lists Alt + H, B for adding borders, but the extra letters A (all borders), N (no border) and M (More Borders), and the letters used inside the dialog, are not listed. Community guides agree on them, though one older list describes N as removing only the outline, so check the result in your version.
steps: Select the cells you want to change.
Press Alt and let go, then press H, then B, then A to add borders around every cell. Use H, B, N instead to remove the borders.
Each key is pressed on its own, in order. Do not hold them down together.

For more control, press Alt, H, B, M to open the Borders tab of the Format Cells dialog. There, hold Alt and press a letter to pick a border: T top, B bottom, L left, R right, H inside horizontal, V inside vertical, O outline, I inside, N none. U and D add the up and down diagonal lines.
Press Enter or click OK to apply it.
If a letter does not match in your version, press Alt and follow the Key Tips (the small letters that appear on the ribbon) to the same command.
taskPhrases: add borders around all cells
remove borders from a range
put a grid around the data
clear cell borders
add only a top or bottom border
put an outline around a selection
notes: Alt, H, B opens the Borders menu on the Home tab. The last letter picks the option inside it.
Borders and gridlines are different things. Borders are formatting you add to cells, while gridlines are the faint lines Excel draws on the sheet.
Inside the More Borders dialog the letters are the underlined ones, so they follow the dialog and not the ribbon.

title: Hide cell values
description: Make a cell look empty while its value stays in it, using the custom format ;;;
steps: Select the cells whose values you want to hide.
Right-click and choose Format Cells (or press Ctrl + 1).
On the Number tab, choose Custom.
In the Type box, enter ;;; (three semicolons) and click OK.
To show the values again, set the cells back to General or another number format.
taskPhrases: make the text in a cell invisible
hide the value of a cell without deleting it
hide helper cell values
notes: The value stays in the cell. It still shows in the formula bar when you select the cell, and formulas can still use it.
Anyone who selects the cell can see the value in the formula bar, so this hides it from view but does not protect it.
It is handy for helper cells or calculations you do not want to show.

title: Paste as a linked picture
description: Paste a live picture of some cells somewhere else, and it updates when the cells change.

keys.label: Paste as a linked picture
keys.windows: Alt then H then V then I

unofficial: Alt, H, V, I is not listed on Microsoft’s pages. It follows the ribbon (Home > Paste > Linked Picture), and community guides give the same letters. Microsoft documents linking a range to a picture through the Camera command instead, so check the keys in your version.
steps: Select the cells you want a picture of and press Ctrl + C.
Click the cell or sheet where the picture should go.
Press Alt and let go, then press H, then V, then I, one key at a time.
Change a value in the original cells. The picture updates to match.
If a letter does not match in your version, press Alt and follow the Key Tips (the small letters that appear on the ribbon) to the same command.
taskPhrases: paste a live picture of a range
show a copy of some cells that updates itself
lay out a report from cells on other sheets
notes: The picture is a live copy of the cells: it follows changes in the original cells.
It helps you see how changing one cell far away affects results elsewhere in a large workbook, or lay out a neat report.
Microsoft’s documented way to link cells to a picture is the Camera command, which you add to the Quick Access Toolbar first.

title: Highlight duplicates
description: Colour every repeated value in a range so duplicates stand out.

keys.windows: Alt then H then L then H then D

unofficial: Alt, H, L, H, D is not listed in Microsoft’s shortcut list. It follows the ribbon menus (Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Duplicate Values), and community guides agree on the letters.
steps: Select the range you want to check.
Press Alt and let go, then press H, then L, then H, then D, one key at a time.
In the box that opens, choose how the duplicates should look, then confirm.
If a letter does not match in your version, press Alt and follow the Key Tips (the small letters that appear on the ribbon) to the same command.
taskPhrases: highlight repeated values in a column
find duplicates in a list
mark duplicate entries
colour duplicate cells
notes: This only colours the duplicates. It does not delete them.
To list each value only once, use UNIQUE. To count how often a value appears, use COUNTIF.
Excel has no single dedicated shortcut for this, so the sequence walks through the ribbon menus one step at a time.

title: MIN
description: Returns the smallest number in a set of values.
explanation: Finds the smallest number in {number1}.

arguments.name: number1
arguments.description: The first number, cell or range to check.

arguments.name: number2
arguments.description: More numbers, cells or ranges to check. You can use up to 255 arguments in total.
arguments.clause: It also checks {number2}.

taskPhrases: find the lowest value
find the smallest number
get the minimum of a column
cheapest price in a list
notes: Text, true/false values and empty cells inside a range are ignored.
If there are no numbers at all, MIN returns 0.
To include true/false values and number-like text, use MINA.

title: COUNTA
description: Counts the cells that are not empty.
explanation: Counts the cells in {value1} that are not empty.

arguments.name: value1
arguments.description: The first value, cell or range to count.

arguments.name: value2
arguments.description: More values, cells or ranges to count. You can use up to 255 arguments in total.
arguments.clause: It also counts the non-empty cells in {value2}.

taskPhrases: count cells that are not empty
count how many cells have something in them
count filled cells
count non blank cells
notes: COUNTA counts any cell that holds something: numbers, text, true/false values, errors, and even empty text ("") returned by a formula. It does not count truly empty cells.
To count only the cells that hold numbers, use COUNT.
To count only the cells that meet a condition, use COUNTIF or COUNTIFS.
You can use up to 255 arguments.

title: SUMIF
description: Adds up the values that meet one condition.
explanation: Adds up the cells in {range} that match {criteria}.

arguments.name: range
arguments.description: The cells to test against the condition.

arguments.name: criteria
arguments.description: The condition, such as "North", ">100" or a cell reference. Text, and conditions with symbols, go in double quotes.

arguments.name: sum_range
arguments.description: The cells to add, if they are different from range. If left out, Excel adds the cells in range.
arguments.clause: Instead of adding {range}, it adds the cells in {sum_range} that sit alongside the matches.

taskPhrases: add up values that match one condition
total for one region
sum only the rows that match
sum numbers if another column equals something
notes: If you leave sum_range out, SUMIF adds the cells in range itself, which are also the cells being tested.
sum_range should be the same size and shape as range. If it is not, SUMIF starts at the first cell of sum_range and uses the size of range, which can give surprising results.
Wildcards work in the condition: ? matches one character and * matches any run of characters. Put ~ in front to match the symbol itself.
SUMIF gives wrong results when it matches text longer than 255 characters.
For more than one condition, use SUMIFS. The argument order differs: sum_range is last in SUMIF but first in SUMIFS.

title: ROUND
description: Rounds a number to the number of digits you choose.
explanation: Rounds {number} to {num_digits} digits. A positive number keeps that many decimal places, 0 gives a whole number, and a negative number rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

arguments.name: number
arguments.description: The number to round.

arguments.name: num_digits
arguments.description: How many digits to round to. Positive keeps that many decimal places, 0 gives a whole number, and negative rounds to the left of the decimal point.

taskPhrases: round a number to 2 decimal places
round to the nearest whole number
round to the nearest ten
reduce the decimal places
notes: A negative num_digits rounds to the left of the decimal point. For example, ROUND(21.5, -1) gives 20, and ROUND(626.3, -3) gives 1000.
To always round up (away from zero) use ROUNDUP, and to always round down (toward zero) use ROUNDDOWN. To round to a multiple such as 0.5, use MROUND.
ROUND changes the value itself. Number formatting only changes how a number looks.

title: NETWORKDAYS
description: Counts the working days between two dates.
explanation: Counts the working days from {start_date} to {end_date}, leaving out weekends.

arguments.name: start_date
arguments.description: The first date.

arguments.name: end_date
arguments.description: The last date.

arguments.name: holidays
arguments.description: Dates to leave out, such as public holidays, as a range of cells that hold dates.
arguments.clause: It also leaves out the dates in {holidays}.

taskPhrases: count working days between two dates
calculate business days
how many weekdays between dates
exclude weekends and holidays
notes: Microsoft’s page does not say which days count as the weekend or whether the start and end dates are included. By default Excel treats Saturday and Sunday as the weekend and counts both dates. Use NETWORKDAYS.INTL to choose different weekend days.
Enter dates with the DATE function or as the results of other formulas. Dates typed as text can cause problems, and a date that is not valid returns #VALUE!.
In the sample, 2 Nov to 13 Nov 2026 is two full working weeks, so the result is 10. Adding the holiday on 11 Nov makes it 9.

title: RIGHT
description: Returns the last characters of a piece of text.
explanation: Takes text from the end of {text}.

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: The text, or the cell that contains it.

arguments.name: num_chars
arguments.description: How many characters to take. If left out, it takes 1.
arguments.clause: It takes the last {num_chars} characters.

taskPhrases: get the last few characters of a cell
extract the last 4 digits
take the end of a code
notes: If num_chars is left out, RIGHT returns just the last character.
num_chars must be zero or more. If it is longer than the text, RIGHT returns all of the text.

title: MID
description: Returns characters from the middle of a piece of text.
explanation: Takes {num_chars} characters from {text}, starting at character number {start_num}.

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: The text, or the cell that contains it.

arguments.name: start_num
arguments.description: The position of the first character to take. The first character is number 1.

arguments.name: num_chars
arguments.description: How many characters to take.

taskPhrases: get characters from the middle of a cell
extract part of a code
take text starting at a position
notes: The first character of the text is position 1.
If start_num is past the end of the text, MID returns empty text. If start_num is less than 1, or num_chars is negative, it returns #VALUE!.
If num_chars asks for more characters than remain, MID returns what is left.

title: LEN
description: Counts the characters in a piece of text.
explanation: Counts the characters in {text}, including spaces.

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: The text, or the cell that contains it. Spaces count as characters.

taskPhrases: count the characters in a cell
find the length of text
check how long a code is
count letters
notes: Spaces and punctuation count as characters.
An empty cell gives 0.
LEN helps spot hidden extra spaces: if a name looks 7 characters long but LEN says 9, there are stray spaces. TRIM removes them.

title: IFS
description: Checks several conditions in order and returns the result for the first one that is true.
explanation: Checks whether {logical_test1} is true. If it is, it shows {value_if_true1}.

arguments.name: logical_test1
arguments.description: The first condition to test.

arguments.name: value_if_true1
arguments.description: What to show if the first condition is true.

arguments.name: logical_test2
arguments.description: A second condition, checked only if the first one is false.
arguments.clause: Otherwise it checks {logical_test2} and, if that is true, shows {value_if_true2}.

arguments.name: value_if_true2
arguments.description: What to show if the second condition is true.

arguments.name: logical_test3
arguments.description: A third condition. Use TRUE here to catch everything that did not match earlier.
arguments.clause: Then it checks {logical_test3} and, if that is true, shows {value_if_true3}.

arguments.name: value_if_true3
arguments.description: What to show if the third condition is true.

taskPhrases: check several conditions in order
replace nested if statements
assign a grade based on a score
return different results for different ranges
notes: If none of the conditions is true, IFS returns #N/A. To avoid that, end with TRUE as the last test and put your default result after it.
IFS can replace several nested IFs and is easier to read. Microsoft still advises against stacking too many conditions, because they get hard to build, test and update.
You can use up to 127 conditions.
Available in Microsoft 365, Excel 2019, Excel 2021 and Excel 2024.

title: IFNA
description: Replaces a #N/A error with a value you choose.
explanation: Calculates {value}. If that gives a #N/A error, it shows {value_if_na} instead.

arguments.name: value
arguments.description: The formula or value to check for a #N/A error.

arguments.name: value_if_na
arguments.description: What to show if the result is #N/A.

taskPhrases: replace #n/a with a message
show not found when a lookup fails
hide n/a errors from a lookup
notes: It only replaces the #N/A error, which is what a lookup returns when it finds nothing. To handle every error type, use IFERROR.
An empty cell used for either argument is treated as empty text ("").

title: Go To Special: select cells by type
description: Select only the cells of one kind inside your selection, such as blanks, formulas or visible cells.
unofficial: The Numbers, Text, Logicals and Errors tick boxes under Constants and Formulas are not listed on Microsoft’s page, which only says the boxes under Formulas set the type of formula. They appear in the dialog in current Excel, but check them in your version.
steps: Select the cells to search. A single cell searches the whole worksheet, while a range, row or column searches only inside it.
Press Ctrl + G (or F5 on Windows), then click Special. You can also use Home > Find & Select > Go To.
Choose what to select, such as Blanks, Constants, Formulas or Visible cells only, then click OK. Excel selects only the matching cells inside your selection.
For Constants or Formulas, tick the kinds you want first. For example, select a row of names and numbers, choose Constants, and tick only Numbers to keep just the numbers selected.
Format, delete, fill or copy just those cells. To cancel the selection, click any cell.
taskPhrases: select only the numbers in a range
select all the blank cells at once
select only cells with formulas
select only the text cells
copy only the visible cells
find cells with conditional formatting
pick out one kind of cell from a selection
notes: On Mac, Microsoft also lists Shift + Cmd + * for Visible cells only.

options.name: Constants
options.text: Cells that hold a typed-in value rather than a formula. Tick Numbers, Text, Logicals or Errors to keep only those kinds.

options.name: Formulas
options.text: Cells that contain formulas. The same four ticks narrow them down by the kind of result.

options.name: Current region
options.text: The whole block of data around the active cell, such as an entire list.

options.name: Current array
options.text: The whole array, if the active cell is part of one.

options.name: Objects
options.text: Charts, buttons and other graphical objects on the sheet, including those in text boxes.

options.name: Row differences
options.text: Cells in a selected row that differ from the active cell.

options.name: Column differences
options.text: Cells in a selected column that differ from the active cell.

options.name: Precedents
options.text: Cells that the formula in the active cell uses. Direct only picks the cells it refers to; All levels also picks the cells those depend on.

options.name: Dependents
options.text: Cells with formulas that use the active cell. Direct only picks formulas that refer to it; All levels also picks formulas that depend on those.

options.name: Last cell
options.text: The last cell on the sheet that contains data or formatting.

options.name: Visible cells only
options.text: Only the cells you can see in a range that crosses hidden rows or columns.

options.name: Conditional formats
options.text: Cells that have conditional formatting. All picks every one; Same picks only those that share the active cell’s formatting.

options.name: Data validation
options.text: Cells that have data validation rules. All picks every one; Same picks only those that share the active cell’s rules.

title: Paste values only
description: Paste what a cell shows, without its formula or formatting.

keys.label: Open Paste Special, then choose Values
Paste values straight away
keys.windows: Alt then H then V then V

unofficial: Alt, H, V, V is not listed in Microsoft’s shortcut list. It follows the ribbon (Home > Paste > Values), and community guides give the same letters. The documented route is Ctrl + Alt + V, then V.
steps: Select the cells and press Ctrl + C (Cmd + C on Mac).
Click the cell where the values should go.
Press Ctrl + Alt + V to open Paste Special, choose Values (or press V), then click OK.
Or press Alt and let go, then H, then V, then V, one key at a time, to paste values in one go.
taskPhrases: paste only the values and not the formulas
turn formulas into plain values
copy a result without its formula
notes: Pasting values turns the result into plain text or numbers, so it no longer updates when the original cells change.
On Mac, Microsoft lists no values-only shortcut. Use the Paste Special dialog.

title: Turn filters on or off
description: Add filter buttons to a table of data, or remove them, from the keyboard.
unofficial: Ctrl + Shift + L is not listed in Microsoft’s Windows shortcut list, though its Mac list gives Cmd + Shift + F or Ctrl + Shift + L. It is widely used on Windows too, but check it in your version.
steps: Click a cell inside your data. Make sure each column has a header.
Press Ctrl + Shift + L. Filter buttons appear on the headers.
Click a button to sort the column or pick the values to show.
Press the same keys again to remove the filter buttons.
taskPhrases: add filter buttons to a table
turn filters on and off quickly
show only some rows of my data
notes: This changes what you see on the sheet. The FILTER function is different: it builds a separate list of results with a formula.
Pressing Ctrl + A first selects the whole block of data, which is a handy way to be sure the filter covers all of it.

title: Edit a cell
description: Start editing the selected cell without double-clicking it.
steps: Select the cell.
Press F2. The cursor goes to the end of what is in the cell, and you can type or fix it.
Press Enter to save the change, or Esc to cancel.
taskPhrases: edit a cell without double clicking
change a formula from the keyboard
put the cursor inside a cell
notes: It also works on formulas, so it is a quick way to fix one.

title: Format Cells
description: Open the dialog with every format setting for the selected cells.
steps: Select the cells you want to format.
Press Ctrl + 1 (Cmd + 1 on Mac). The Format Cells dialog opens.
Use the tabs, such as Number, Alignment, Font, Border and Fill, then click OK.
taskPhrases: open the format cells window
change how cells look from one dialog
set borders and fill from one dialog
notes: Right-clicking a cell and choosing Format Cells opens the same dialog.

title: New line in a cell
description: Start a new line inside one cell instead of moving to the next cell.
steps: Double-click the cell or press F2 to start editing it.
Type the first line of text.
Press Alt + Enter (Ctrl + Option + Return on Mac) to start a new line in the same cell.
Type the next line, then press Enter to finish.
taskPhrases: put two lines of text in one cell
start a new line inside a cell
add a second line to a cell
notes: If the cell still shows one long line, turn on Wrap Text for it on the Home tab.

title: Currency, percent and date formats
description: Switch the selected cells to a number, currency, percentage or date format.
steps: Select the cells you want to format.
Press the keys for the format you want. Each one needs Shift, because the symbol is on a number key (1, 4, 5 and 3).
taskPhrases: format a column as currency
show values as percentages
change cells to a date format
notes: Percentage turns 0.25 into 25%, so apply it to cells that hold fractions, not to numbers that are already percentages.
For other formats, open Format Cells with Ctrl + 1.

title: Switch between sheets
description: Move to the next or previous worksheet without clicking the tabs.
steps: Press the Next sheet keys to move one sheet to the right.
Press the Previous sheet keys to move one sheet to the left.
taskPhrases: go to the next worksheet
move between sheets with the keyboard
switch tabs in a workbook

title: Keep leading zeros
description: Stop Excel dropping the zeros at the start of codes such as 00123 or 0412.
steps: Click the cell and type an apostrophe (’) first, then the number, for example ’00123. Excel treats it as text and keeps the zeros.
To do it for a whole column, select it first, open Format Cells with Ctrl + 1, choose Text on the Number tab, then type the numbers.
If the zeros are already gone, use the formula =TEXT(A2, "00000") to add them back. The number of zeros is the total length you want.
taskPhrases: stop excel removing the zero at the start
keep the zeros in a code
show 00123 instead of 123
notes: Text formatting must be set before you type the numbers. It does not bring back zeros that were already removed.
Excel keeps only 15 digits of a number. For longer codes, such as card numbers, use the Text format.
